fact: The Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board said on 3 September 2025 that over 90 percent of Pennsylvania sports wagering is placed on online platforms, and that the Board itself takes bettor complaints and disputes against licensed operators and investigates them, a service it cannot offer if the problem is with an offshore site.

Pennsylvania runs self-exclusion as four separate Board lists (casinos and offsite venues such as off-track betting, interactive gambling, video gaming terminals, and fantasy contests); casino bans of one or five years stay in force until you ask to come off, the others lapse when the chosen term ends, and breaking an exclusion means winnings are confiscated. The Board's page does not name a sports-wagering list, but its September 2025 release says the self-exclusion programme blocks access to all Board-regulated online betting sites.

The Pennsylvania Act (4 Pa.C.S. Chapter 13C, added 30 October 2017 as Act 42) defines a sporting event as a professional or collegiate sports or athletic event or a motor race event, and defines sports wagering to include bets on athletes' individual performance statistics.

Hollywood Casino at Penn National Race Course took Pennsylvania's first legal sports bet on 15 November 2018, a $20 wager on the Steelers to win the Super Bowl (secondary: The Philadelphia Inquirer, 3 December 2018).
West Virginia's first legal sports bet was taken on 30 August 2018 at Hollywood Casino at Charles Town Races (secondary: WCHS-TV, 30 August 2018).
State law allows at most five sports wagering licences, available only to the state's racetrack and historic resort casinos, and every sports wager is a West Virginia Lottery game owned by the state.
Each West Virginia licence holder may run no more than three individually branded online sportsbook sites and apps (rule 179-9-12.1).

West Virginia's Sports Wagering Act defines sports events to include any collegiate sport or athletic event and defines sports wagering to include bets on athletes' individual performance statistics; it also excludes daily fantasy sports.

The Racing and Gaming Commission's sports wagering regulations (K.A.R. 112-201 through 112-204), whose current text carries an effective date of 11 September 2026 after temporary rules effective 12 August 2022, ban sportsbooks from describing an advertisement or promotion as free of risk.

Kansas has its own Sports Wagering Exclusion Program, run by the Racing and Gaming Commission and separate from the casino Voluntary Exclusion Program: enrolling disables all active sports wagering accounts, blocks new ones and cannot be undone early, casino exclusion participants who joined after 1 September 2022 are barred from sports wagering too, and if you self-exclude with a bet still open it settles and any winnings or pushed stake go to the state problem gambling grant fund.

Kansas law (2022 Senate Bill 84) limits each of the four state-owned casinos to three sports wagering platforms, forbids any line of credit to a bettor, requires you to be physically in Kansas to bet online, and does not treat an event as a sporting event if most of its participants are under 18.

Kansas sportsbooks at the four state-owned casinos began taking in-person and mobile bets on 1 September 2022, with the official opening on 8 September (secondary: KWCH-TV, 18 August 2022, reporting Governor Laura Kelly's announcement).
North Carolina law does not authorise sports wagering on youth sports, or on injuries, penalties, the outcome of disciplinary proceedings, or the outcome of replay reviews.

A North Carolina online operator can only be licensed if it has a written designation agreement with a professional sports team, a motorsports facility, a facility hosting a yearly professional golf event, or a NASCAR or golf sanctioning body, and each of those partners may sign with only one operator.

The Commission's Voluntary Exclusion Program lets you pick one year, three years, five years or lifetime, covers sports and pari-mutuel wagering, does not reach tribal lands, and early removal needs a reinstatement session followed by a 30 day wait.

North Carolina's Commission rules bar operators from calling a promotion "free" unless it costs the player nothing, or free of risk if the player must lose or risk their own money to use it or withdraw winnings.

Vermont's law lets the state contract two to six mobile sportsbooks; the Department of Liquor and Lottery chose three (DraftKings, FanDuel and Fanatics Sportsbook) and mobile betting launched on 11 January 2024. There is no retail option.

Vermont bars wagers on any college game involving a college team based in Vermont unless it is part of a tournament, and bars any high school or college event played in Vermont; bets on athletes' individual performance statistics are part of the legal definition of sports wagering.

Vermont forbids funding a sports wagering account with a credit card (31 V.S.A. 1340(d)(2)) and allows one account per person per operator; the Board's procedures, adopted 13 May 2026 and dated 1 October 2026, also bar wagers on injuries or penalties, bar calling a promotion free of risk if you must risk your own money, and block betting once lifetime deposits pass $2,500, and again each year after, until you acknowledge it and can set limits or close the account.

Vermont's statewide self-exclusion list is run by the Department; you choose 1, 3 or 5 years or lifetime, a lifetime choice cannot be undone, and fantasy sports need a separate opt-in with each fantasy operator.
Wyoming taxes online sports wagering at 10 percent of the prior month's revenue, and the first $300,000 each fiscal year goes to county programmes that prevent and treat problem gambling.
Wyoming's minimum age for online sports wagering is 18, not 21 (W.S. 9-24-105; the helpline file already carries 18).

Wyoming's statute counts collegiate events as sporting events, its rules exclude only events where most athletes are under 18, and its rules ban wagers on the injury of a participant; I found no in-state college ban in the text read.

Wyoming's Gaming Commission voted unanimously on 22 November 2024 to put anyone found guilty of harassing an athlete on the state's involuntary exclusion list (rule text, Chapter 8 Section 3(a)(i); the vote date is from the trade outlet reprinted on the Commission's page, so secondary).

Maryland has barred player-specific proposition bets on college participants since 1 March 2024, a directive from the Lottery and Gaming agency to sportsbooks rather than a statute; a 2026 bill (HB 518) would have written it into law and its page shows no action past Senate second reading, so I found no sign it was enacted.

Maryland's sports wagering regulations bar bets on high school events, bar bets on any amateur event (college included) unless the Commission specifically approves it, bar wagers on injuries, penalties, player disciplinary rulings and replay reviews, and cap any one bettor's wager on one event at $5,000,000.
Sports winnings in Maryland that go unclaimed for 182 days after the wager is won revert to the state's Problem Gambling Fund.
Maryland's Voluntary Exclusion Program covers sports wagering in person and online, the minimum stay on the list is two years (or lifetime), and removal is never automatic.

Illinois bars every wager on a sports event involving an Illinois collegiate team, in person as well as online, because the in-person exception (tier 1 wagers not tied to an individual athlete) ran only until 1 July 2024; it also bars minor league events and kindergarten through 12th grade events. The CSV note says "No online wagers", which understates this.

Since 1 July 2025 Illinois has charged each online sportsbook a wager tax of $0.25 on each of its first 20,000,000 online wagers a year and $0.50 on each wager after that; it is levied on the operator, not the bettor, and a further 2 percent of adjusted gross receipts on wagers placed inside Cook County goes to the county's criminal justice system.

Illinois sports bettors who self-exclude use the Gaming Board's Self-Exclusion Program, which has covered sports wagering since the 2019 Sports Wagering Act, and enrolment must be done in person (about 30 to 45 minutes, photo ID required) at Gaming Board offices in the casinos or other sanctioned sites, including some in Iowa.

Colorado made it unlawful for an internet sportsbook to accept a credit card deposit, directly or through an account funded by a credit card, under Senate Bill 26-131 (signed 1 June 2026, effective date set by the act as 12 August 2026, with a maximum Commission penalty of $25,000); on 15 October 2026 the Division of Gaming's Bulletin 17 told operators to decline any prepaid card deposit whose funding source they cannot verify was not a credit card.
The same Colorado act caps an internet sportsbook at six separate deposits per person per gaming day and bars it from sending push notifications or texts that solicit bets or deposits.
Colorado voters approved Proposition DD, which legalised and taxed sports betting to fund state water projects, on 5 November 2019 by 800,745 yes votes to 756,712 no.
Colorado keeps one Exclusion List covering casinos and sportsbooks; a person on it may not participate or collect winnings and forfeits money wagered after being added.

New York limits credit card funding to $2,500 per year for each account with each operator, and once an account's lifetime deposits pass $2,500 the operator must block all betting until the bettor acknowledges it, after which the bettor can set limits or close the account.

New York's age is set by statute: a "minor" is anyone under 21 (fills the blank min_age), and mobile bets are legally accepted by equipment at a licensed commercial casino, with the Gaming Commission, not the operators, controlling which sports and leagues are on the menu.

In a letter to leagues dated 4 February 2026 the Gaming Commission said it is re-examining all game-specific individual player proposition wagers and single-game multi-leg individual player parlays and will prohibit some outright if its review requires it.

New York's Voluntary Self-Exclusion covers sports wagering along with all other New York gaming, lasts one year, three years, five years or lifetime, needs a form and photo handed in at a gaming facility, at Commission headquarters, or mailed notarised, and any winnings made while excluded are forfeited.

Connecticut allows only three online sports betting skins by statute (one each for the Mashantucket Pequot Tribe and the Mohegan Tribe, one for the Connecticut Lottery Corporation outside the reservations), and the Department of Consumer Protection's FAQ currently lists three platforms: DraftKings, FanDuel and Bet Fanatics.

Beyond the college rule already on the page, Connecticut teams can only be backed to win a tournament of four or more intercollegiate teams, the wager must cover all the tournament's games and be placed before it starts, and single games involving a Connecticut team are never allowed, even inside a tournament.
Connecticut allows credit cards for betting but limits a person to one debit card or one credit card per account and requires operators to put a monetary limit on credit card use.

Connecticut's self-exclusion list lets you choose one year, five years or lifetime, bars you from collecting winnings or recovering losses, and lets operators extend the ban to their offerings in other states.

Michigan's Lawful Sports Betting Act lets the Gaming Control Board license only holders of a Michigan commercial casino license and Indian tribes that lawfully run class III casinos in the state, with no more than one sports betting operator license each (MCL 432.406); internet betting could not start until at least one casino licensee and one tribe had been licensed.

Under MCL 432.404 each Michigan sports betting operator may use no more than one internet sports betting platform, an online wager counts in law as gambling at that operator's Michigan casino wherever you are when you place it, and no one may put sports betting devices in bars, clubs or other places of public accommodation (operators may still offer them inside their own casino).

Michigan's casino ban is the Gaming Control Board's list of disassociated persons (MCL 432.225): a name stays on for life unless, no sooner than 5 years after placement, the person files the Board's removal form; while listed, entering a casino is criminal trespassing punishable by up to 1 year in jail and a $1,000 fine, and the Board can confiscate any winnings for the compulsive gaming prevention fund.

For online sports betting Michigan law sets up a separate statewide responsible gaming database (MCL 432.412): the Board's executive director can add people for gaming-related convictions or law violations or because they are on a current exclusion list in another US jurisdiction, operators must offer both temporary and permanent self-exclusion plus deposit, wager and playing-time limits, and the lists are exempt from Michigan's Freedom of Information Act.

Massachusetts law bars sportsbooks from accepting a credit card or a wager from anyone under 21 (G.L. c. 23N, s. 13(d)), and a mobile wager must be initiated, received and made inside the Commonwealth by someone physically there.

Massachusetts operators may not offer bets on Massachusetts college teams unless the team is playing in a collegiate tournament, may not take bets on such a team before it qualifies for one, and may not offer bets on awards to individual college athletes; the Gaming Commission says retail betting began at the casinos on January 31, 2023 and mobile betting on March 10, 2023.

The Gaming Commission's voluntary self-exclusion offers one, three or five years or lifetime (lifetime only after completing a shorter term), with casino gaming, sports wagering and iLottery as separate lists you can join alone or together; terms can be extended but not shortened, a term never ends by itself, and you stay excluded until you complete a reinstatement session.

On launch day, January 31, 2023, Springfield Mayor Domenic Sarno placed the first legal sports wager at MGM Springfield at 10:01 a.m., and at Plainridge Park former Patriot Rob Ninkovich placed the ceremonial first bet just after 1 p.m., on the Bruins to win the Stanley Cup, according to the Gaming Commission.

Louisiana voters decided sports betting parish by parish on November 3, 2020: 55 of 64 parishes said yes, while Caldwell, Catahoula, Franklin, Jackson, LaSalle, Sabine, Union, West Carroll and Winn said no, and you must be physically in an approving parish to place any bet, mobile included; the Gaming Control Board's 2025 report dates mobile betting to January 28, 2022.

Louisiana law (La. R.S. 27:608) bans sportsbooks from taking or paying bets on injuries or penalties, on the outcome of an athlete's disciplinary rulings, or on replay reviews, and an operator must collect identifying information from anyone placing a single in-person wager of $10,000 or more.

Louisiana self-exclusion is signed in person before a State Police Gaming Enforcement agent at a field office in Baton Rouge, Breaux Bridge, Lake Charles, New Orleans or Bossier City; it covers all casinos and sports wagering platforms for at least five years, after which the name stays on until you ask, a hearing is held and the Board decides; winnings made while excluded are withheld and paid to the state, and entering a casino can mean arrest.

Sportsbook complaints and disputes in Louisiana go to the Louisiana State Police Gaming Enforcement Division, which takes them on a separate online Complaint/Dispute by Gaming Patron form for sports wagering, by phone at (225) 925-1900, or by mail to 7919 Independence Blvd., Baton Rouge.

Florida law (s. 285.710, F.S.) ratifies the 2021 Seminole compact and deems every sports wager, including one placed on a phone or other device by a player anywhere in Florida, to be conducted by the Seminole Tribe where its servers sit on Indian lands; bettors must be 21, and the Florida Gaming Control Commission is the state agency that oversees the compact.

The 2021 compact covers professional and college sports but excludes proposition bets on college sports and events, and all betting must run through sports books operated by the Tribe or its approved management contractor; the Interior Department took no action by August 5, 2021, so the compact was approved by operation of law only to the extent it complies with federal law.

On June 30, 2023 the federal appeals court in Washington (West Flagler Associates v. Haaland, No. 21-5265) reversed the district court ruling against the compact, holding that the compact itself authorizes only the betting that occurs on the Tribe's lands and that whether a patron may lawfully bet from elsewhere in Florida may be a question for Florida's courts.
The US Supreme Court denied the Florida casinos' petition to review that ruling on June 17, 2024 (No. 23-862); Justice Kavanaugh would have taken the case and Justice Jackson took no part.

Under Part VI of the compact a betting dispute with the Seminole sports book is first handled under the Seminole Tribal Gaming Code; if you are still not satisfied you may appeal to the state compliance agency, whose decision binds both you and the Tribe.

Indiana's Voluntary Exclusion Program, run by the Gaming Commission, lasts one year, five years or lifetime, and a lifetime choice can never be removed; it covers every Indiana casino, all sports wagering operators including mobile apps, the off-track betting sites in Clarksville, Indianapolis and New Haven, and Four Winds South Bend under the Pokagon Band compact, and winnings found on a participant at a casino are forfeited as a fine.

An Indiana sportsbook must answer a written complaint within 10 calendar days; if a complaint about your account, how a bet was settled, or illegal activity is still unresolved, you send it with the operator's response to the Gaming Commission's Sports Wagering Division on its patron complaint form. For mobile betting alone, the Commission also runs an Internet Self-Restriction Program of 1 or 5 years that ends only when you ask to come off.

In Indiana only casinos, racinos and off-track betting facilities can hold a sports wagering certificate, and each holder may contract with no more than three branded online sportsbooks (IC 4-38-5-12); you never have to register or deposit in person, may hold accounts with several operators but only one per operator, and betting on high school or other amateur youth events is banned.

Indiana's law (House Enrolled Act 1015-2019) allowed sports wagering from September 1, 2019, and the Gaming Commission's executive director told its November 8, 2019 meeting that mobile betting launched on October 3, 2019 with three companies taking mobile wagers.

New Jersey bans betting on any college game played in New Jersey and on any game involving a New Jersey college team wherever it is played (N.J.S.A. 5:12A-10), though other games in a tournament a New Jersey team is in, and games of an out-of-state tournament with some games in New Jersey, are allowed; all high school events are banned too.

The Division of Gaming Enforcement runs self-exclusion: in person or by video conference you can choose one year, five years or lifetime from Atlantic City casinos, racetrack sportsbooks and all internet gaming and sports wagering, or from internet gaming and sports wagering only; signing up online or through a player account offers only one or five years.

In New Jersey a lifetime self-exclusion can never be removed; after a one-year or five-year term your name stays on the list until you file the Division's removal form, which you may submit only once the term has expired.

New Jersey's first legal sports bets were two $20 wagers Governor Phil Murphy placed at Monmouth Park's sports book on June 14, 2018, one on Germany to win the World Cup and one on the New Jersey Devils to win the next Stanley Cup (Associated Press, via WHYY).

Tennessee's Sports Gaming Act (Public Chapter 507 of 2019) allows only mobile and interactive sports wagering statewide, with no sportsbook locations and no local-option elections; the governor returned the bill without his signature on June 4, 2019.

Tennessee's Sports Wagering Council licenses 12 online sports betting platforms and taxes total wagers rather than revenue, at 1.85% of handle; its executive director told the State Funding Board on November 3, 2025 that Tennessee is the largest online-only market, that it had served cease and desist orders on 20 illegal sportsbooks, and that prediction markets lack protections such as self-exclusion.

The minimum age to place or cash a sports wager in the District of Columbia is 18, not 21; you may not bet on any college event involving a District of Columbia college team, wherever it is played, or on any high school sports.

The Office of Lottery and Gaming's license list (April 30, 2026) shows the three Class A stadium operators, Caesars Sportsbook at Capital One Arena, FanDuel at Audi Field and BetMGM at Nationals Park, licensed for District-wide online and mobile apps, and DraftKings and Fanatics holding temporary Class C District-wide licenses; Class B books take bets, mobile included, only inside their premises.

The Office of Lottery and Gaming itself ran District-wide mobile betting as GambetDC, through its contractor Intralot, everywhere except the Class A two-block zones and the area covered by the federal Shipstead-Luce Act; on April 15, 2024 GambetDC's app was converted to FanDuel as Intralot's subcontractor, the District taking 40% of gross gaming revenue, and OLG also ran self-service kiosks at 63 licensed retail locations, per its May 6, 2024 testimony to the DC Council.

DC's self-exclusion, signed in person at the Office of Lottery and Gaming at 2235 Shannon Place SE, runs one year, 18 months, three years, five years or lifetime, and lifetime is open only to someone already on the list for six months; it covers licensed sportsbooks, lottery retailers' gaming areas and DC Lottery sites and apps, ending a term takes an in-person exit session, and an excluded person forfeits money wagered and winnings.

Nevada lets a book register you for a sports wagering account remotely, but under Gaming Commission Regulations 5.225(7) and 22.140(6) you cannot bet until you have shown government photo ID in person to an employee at the book, its casino or, for central-site books, an outstation or affiliated book (or at an off-site spot the Board Chair approves); the remote ID check allowed for other wagering accounts does not apply to sports accounts.

Nevada books may not take bets on the outcome of any election for public office, in Nevada or elsewhere, or on amateur sports other than the Olympics and college sports (Regulation 22.1205); every book's house rules must say that cancelling a wager needs the Gaming Control Board's approval.

In Nevada a casino or book must tell the Gaming Control Board at once about any patron dispute of $500 or more, and for smaller ones must tell you that you can ask the Board to investigate; a Board agent decides whether you are paid and mails the decision within 45 days, and you then have 20 days to petition for reconsideration (NRS 463.362 and 463.363).

Nevada's wagering-account rule (Regulation 5.225(9)) lets you fund an account with cash at the licensee, checks, wire transfer or money order, a debit, prepaid or credit card, a bank transfer, or credit extended by the licensee itself.
